## Model Comparison & Business Evaluation: SVM vs. Neural Networks

We evaluated whether a Feed-Forward Neural Network (NN) provides sufficient operational value over our champion Two-Stage Hurdle Support Vector Machine (SVM) for real-time fleet dispatching at our target resolution: 1-hour buckets across Resolution 6 H3 Hexagons (289,080 cell-hours; test mean demand $\approx 17.6$ trips/hour).

| Architecture / Model | $R^2$ Score | MAE (Trips) | RMSE (Trips) | Boundary Infractions | Operational Complexity |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| **Two-Stage Hurdle SVM (No Weather)** | **0.8751** | 6.44 | **20.31** | **0.0%** (Blocked) | Low–Moderate (~12 min train) |
| **Deep Tuned NN (NB2 Loss)** | 0.8590 | **6.36** | 21.08 | **0.0%** (Exponentiated) | High (Multi-stage sweep) |
| **Historical Mean Benchmark** | 0.8330 | 7.24 | 22.94 | 0.0% | Zero (Lookup table) |
| **Linear SVR Baseline** | 0.6134 | 13.05 | 35.73 | 34.52% (Clipped) | Low (< 1 sec; invalid) |

At our core dispatch horizon, both advanced models comfortably outperform simple linear and historical benchmarks. The Deep Tuned NN achieves the lowest mean absolute error (**6.36 trips/hour**), marginally edging out the Hurdle SVM (**6.44 trips/hour**) by **0.08 trips per cell-hour**. However, the Hurdle SVM significantly outperforms the NN in global variance capture ($R^2 = 0.8751$ vs. $0.8590$) and peak error mitigation ($\text{RMSE} = 20.31$ vs. $21.08$). This discrepancy stems from the NN’s negative binomial (NB2) log-link: its exponential output function $\exp(\cdot)$ causes minor log-space overshoots during high-density demand surges to explode upon exponentiation, inflating squared residuals. Conversely, the Hurdle SVR fits a continuous regression plane directly on active demand, tracking peak surges without numerical instability. Both models successfully eliminate impossible negative demand ($0.0\%$ infractions).

Is the Neural Network worth deploying? For a Chicago fleet operator managing real-time vehicle rebalancing, deploying a Neural Network over the Hurdle SVM is not justified:

1. *Negligible Operational Edge:* A marginal reduction of **0.08 trips/hour** provides no practical advantage when rebalancing fleet vehicles in discrete units.
2. *High Infrastructure & Training Overhead:* Unlike the Hurdle SVM, which trains deterministically in ~12 minutes via Nystroëm landmark approximation, NNs exhibit severe hyperparameter fragility (untuned variants collapsed to negative $R^2$) and require continuous re-tuning, GPU serving infrastructure, and monitoring against exponential prediction drift.
3. *Inferior Surge Forecasting:* Lower $R^2$ and higher RMSE make the NN less reliable for predicting critical high-density demand surges (e.g., event exits, airport waves) where fleet misallocations incur steep opportunity costs.

Our final deployment recommendation is to deploy the **Two-Stage Hurdle SVM (No Weather)**. It maximizes variance capture ($R^2 = 0.8751$), natively prevents negative outputs, and ensures computational stability.Might retain the **Historical Mean Lookup** as a zero-cost backup for low-volume edge cases. Standalone Neural Networks should not be used for 1-hour fleet dispatching due to disproportionate operational overhead and lower variance capture.
